title: Loki: The Problem Inside
subtitle: The gods' best fixer and their worst one — often in the same story

learningObjectives.text: Why is Loki both rescue and ruin?

lokasenna.author: Anonymous Old Norse poets
lokasenna.locator: Lokasenna, stanzas 3-6; local text normalized characters 237167-237900
lokasenna.excerpt: 3. “In shall I go | into Ægir’s hall, For the feast I fain would see; Bale and hatred | I bring to the gods, And their mead with venom I mix.” Eldir spake: 4. “If in thou goest | to Ægir’s hall, And fain the feast wouldst see, And with slander and spite | wouldst sprinkle the gods, Think well lest they wipe it on thee.” Loki spake: 5. “Bethink thee, Eldir, | if thou and I Shall strive with spiteful speech; Richer I grow | in ready words If thou speakest too much to me.” Then Loki went into the hall, but when they who were there saw who had entered, they were all silent. Loki spake: 6. “Thirsty I come | into this thine hall, I, Lopt, from a journey long, To ask of the gods | that one should give Fair mead for a drink to me.

narrativeBlocks.title: The gods' fixer
narrativeBlocks.body: When the gods need a cheat, a shortcut, or a lie that works, Loki is the one they call — he talks them out of debts, tricks giants out of their own plans, and once gives birth to Odin's eight-legged horse.

narrativeBlocks.title: And their ruin
narrativeBlocks.body: The same Loki engineers the death of Baldr — the most loved of the gods — by tricking the blind god Hodr into throwing mistletoe, the one thing in the world that can kill him.

narrativeBlocks.title: The flyting
narrativeBlocks.body: Cornered at a feast, Loki turns on the entire pantheon: he recites each god's private shame aloud — their cowardice, their secrets — until they finally seize him. The poem is called the Lokasenna, 'Loki's Flyting', and it is as brutal as it sounds.

narrativeBlocks.title: Bound until the end
narrativeBlocks.body: The gods bind Loki in a cave beneath the world with the entrails of his own sons, a serpent dripping venom onto his face. His wife holds a bowl to catch the poison; when she empties it, the drips make him writhe — and the earth shakes. He stays bound until Ragnarök, when he will lead the forces that end the gods.

narrativeBlocks.title: Neither hero nor villain
narrativeBlocks.body: Loki is the Norse answer to 'what if the clever one in your camp is also the traitor?' The stories never resolve him — because a group's own wit is always double-edged.

quiz.prompt: Why is Loki dangerous to the gods despite helping them?

choices.text: He sides openly with the giants
The same cleverness that solves their problems also betrays them — he engineers Baldr's death

quiz.explanation: Loki is the inside problem: fixer and traitor at once, unresolved until the end.

choices.text: Bound beneath the world with his sons' entrails, a serpent dripping venom — held until Ragnarök
He is exiled to the sea's edge
He loses his tongue as a forfeit

quiz.explanation: The binding lasts until the world ends — and he will be there to end it.
